content: 1. Women with a family history of breast cancer or those who have breast nodules should be monitored with particular care when using oral contraceptives. 2. Women undergoing treatment for hyperlipidemias should be closely monitored if they choose to use oral contraceptives, as some progestogens may elevate LDL levels and make the management of hyperlipidemias more challenging. 3. If jaundice develops in any woman taking oral contraceptives, the medication should be discontinued immediately. Steroid hormones may be poorly metabolized in patients with impaired liver function. 4. Oral contraceptives may cause fluid retention. They should be prescribed cautiously and with careful monitoring in patients with conditions that could be exacerbated by fluid retention. 5. Patients who experience significant depression while taking oral contraceptives should discontinue the medication and switch to an alternative method of contraception to determine if the symptoms are drug-related. Women with a history of depression should be carefully observed, and the medication should be discontinued if severe depression recurs. 6. Contact lens wearers who develop visual changes or changes in lens tolerance should be evaluated by an ophthalmologist. 7. The use of oral contraceptives has been associated with an increased risk of serious adverse reactions, including thrombophlebitis, arterial thromboembolism, pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction, cerebral hemorrhage, cerebral thrombosis, hypertension, gallbladder disease, and hepatic adenomas or benign liver tumors. 8. There is evidence suggesting a possible association between oral contraceptive use and conditions such as mesenteric thrombosis and retinal thrombosis, though further confirmatory studies are needed. 9. Adverse reactions believed to be drug-related include nausea, vomiting, gastrointestinal symptoms (e.g., abdominal cramps and bloating), breakthrough bleeding, spotting, changes in menstrual flow, amenorrhea, temporary infertility after discontinuation, edema, persistent melasma, breast changes (tenderness, enlargement, secretion), weight changes, changes in cervical erosion and secretion, diminished lactation when used postpartum, cholestatic jaundice, migraines, allergic rash, mental depression, reduced carbohydrate tolerance, vaginal candidiasis, changes in corneal curvature, and intolerance to contact lenses. 10. Adverse reactions reported but not definitively linked to oral contraceptive use include congenital anomalies, premenstrual syndrome, cataracts, optic neuritis, appetite changes, cystitis-like syndrome, headache, nervousness, dizziness, hirsutism, scalp hair loss, erythema multiforme, erythema nodosum, hemorrhagic eruption, vaginitis, porphyria, impaired renal function, hemolytic uremic syndrome, Budd-Chiari syndrome, acne, libido changes, colitis, sickle-cell disease, cerebral-vascular disease with mitral valve prolapse, and lupus-like syndromes. 11. The FDA package insert for Cryselle does not provide information regarding postmarketing experience. 12. Concomitant use of rifampin with oral contraceptives has been associated with reduced efficacy and increased incidence of breakthrough bleeding and menstrual irregularities. Similar, though less pronounced, effects have been suggested with barbiturates, phenylbutazone, phenytoin sodium, and possibly with griseofulvin, ampicillin, and tetracyclines. 13. Oral contraceptives may affect certain laboratory tests, including increased prothrombin and factors VII, VIII, IX, and X; decreased antithrombin III; increased norepinephrine-induced platelet aggregability; increased thyroid-binding globulin (TBG) leading to elevated total thyroid hormone levels; and increased sex-binding globulins, resulting in elevated circulating sex steroids and corticoids, though free or biologically active levels remain unchanged. Triglycerides may be increased, glucose tolerance may be decreased, and serum folate levels may be depressed, which could be clinically significant if pregnancy occurs shortly after discontinuation. 14. Oral contraceptives are classified as Pregnancy Category X by the FDA, indicating they should not be used during pregnancy. There is no FDA or Australian guidance on their use during labor and delivery. 15. Small amounts of oral contraceptive steroids have been detected in the milk of nursing mothers, with some reported adverse effects on the child, including jaundice and breast enlargement. Oral contraceptives given postpartum may interfere with lactation by reducing the quantity and quality of breast milk. Nursing mothers should be advised to use alternative contraception until they have completely weaned their child. 16. The safety and efficacy of norgestrel and ethinyl estradiol tablets have been established in women of reproductive age. These are expected to be the same for postpubertal adolescents under 16 and users aged 16 and older. Use before menarche is not indicated. 17. There is no FDA guidance on the use of norgestrel/ethinyl estradiol in geriatric patients, specific gender populations, racial populations, patients with renal or hepatic impairment, or immunocompromised patients. 18. Oral contraceptives are administered orally. The FDA package insert for Cryselle does not provide information regarding drug monitoring. 19. Serious ill effects have not been reported following acute ingestion of large doses of oral contraceptives by young children. Overdosage may cause nausea, and withdrawal bleeding may occur in females. 20. There is limited information regarding the pharmacology of norgestrel/ethinyl estradiol.
